newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing trial hears gruesome testimony.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing trial hears gruesome testimony.

text.p: A medical examiner testified on Thursday that the left leg from an Oklahoma City bombing victim had never been identified, possibly opening the way for the defence to claim the bomber may have died in the blast.

On the first day of the defence's case, Oklahoma State Medical Examiner Fred Jordan testified about the gruesome task of identifying and matching body parts that were severed in the April 19, 1995, bombing.
Timothy McVeigh is accused of blowing up the Alfred. P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people. He has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.
The defence brought the medical examiner to the stand as it began its attempt to break down the well-crafted case of the prosecution, which rested Wednesday after 137 witnesses.
Jordan testified that originally 98 body parts had been recovered, but through the efforts of an anthropologist who matched up some of the parts, the figure was reduced to 71.
Jordan said 14 legs were recovered from the rubble of the blast and 13 of them were later matched to bodies missing limbs. "There is one left leg, we do not know where it belongs," he testified.
In March 1996, the body of bombing victim Lakesha Levy, 21, was exhumed. A severed left leg she had been buried with was removed and another leg found in the building debris was put in her casket.
But despite sophisticated scientific analysis and the use of world renowned experts, Jordan said authorities were unable to match the extra leg to any bombing victim.
DNA tests were not possible because the leg had been embalmed, he said.

He said it was his impression that the leg belonged to a woman because it looked as if it had been shaved, but he said scientists could not be sure. He estimated the leg belonged to a person with a height of between 5-feet-4-inches (1.62 metres) and 5-feet-6-inches (167 metres).
Under questioning by chief defence attorney Stephen Jones, Jordan said he had read scientific articles about cases where bodies had disintegrated in explosions, except for a single piece of anatomy.

After the bombing the FBI launched a nationwide manhunt for a second suspect referred to as "John Doe No. 2," but never found him. The defence has suggested the leg could have belonged to the bomber who was blown to pieces in the blast.
With earlier witnesses, the defence tried to create doubt about testimony that linked the Ryder truck used in the blast to McVeigh.

Two defence witnesses testified that three days before the bombing they saw a Ryder truck at a Junction City, Kansas, motel where McVeigh is believed to have stayed. The prosecution maintains McVeigh did not rent the truck until the following day.
The witnesses, Herta King and Renda Truong, told the court they were sure about the day because it was Easter Sunday, April 16, 1995.
The prosecution has previously presented a witness who identified McVeigh as the man who rented the truck Monday, April 17, two days before the bombing.
